newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Hungary's Suranyi sees snag in EU inflation goals.
newsitem.headline: Hungary's Suranyi sees snag in EU inflation goals.

text.p: The head of Hungary's central bank said on Thursday that the European Union could not expect new members from Central Europe to meet Maastricht criteria on inflation "in the foreseeable future".
National Bank President Gyorgy Suranyi said Hungary was committed to meeting the EU's Maastricht convergence criteria, but certain criteria could not be met in the short term.

"If inflation is going to be fluctuating between one and two percent in the European Union this is something that is unrealistic in the foreseeable future from the point of view of the transition countries," he told a conference to mark the 50th anniversary of the Marshall Plan that helped rebuild Europe after World War Two.
Suranyi told Reuters that productivity was increasing quickly in post-communist economies, producing a higher rate of growth than in mature economies and an accompanying rise in nominal wages.
He said this meant nominal wage growth would correspond with productivity growth, since there was downward rigidity in nominal wages.
"So all in all due to the close linkage between productivity growth and nominal wage hikes and the unified labour market, inflation has to be inevitably somewhat higher (than in matured economies)."
Suranyi said that although inflation was too high at 18.6 percent, he was satisfied that it had come down from a peak 31 percent at end-1995 and that the downward trend was sustainable.

At the same time, he said, the fiscal deficit has been cut to around four percent of GDP from nine percent and the current account balance of payments deficit has fallen to around 3.6 percent (at end-1996) from 9.4 percent.
Suranyi said Hungary's high inflation had been an unavoidable consequence of a series of major economic structural adjustments after the end of communism.
He compared Hungary's position with that of developed economies in the 1970s, when sharp oil price rises caused a substantial acceleration of inflation, often into double figures.

"It we look at our shocks, our (former Soviet and East European) export market collapsed, the ownership structure was absolutely reshuffled, domestic demand dropped dramatically and the whole external and internal trade has been restructured. It is really not a surprise that inflation has accelerated. It was impossible to avoid."
